Cromwell Tower.lede: Cromwell's only link to the Barbican is a wedding at the local church in 1620.
Cromwell Tower.namesake: He married Elizabeth Bourchier at St Giles Cripplegate in 1620. That is the one tie between him and the Barbican.
Cromwell Tower.setting: A triangular tower at the corner of Beech Street and Silk Street, the easternmost of the three. Each flat has its living room in a corner.
Cromwell Tower.inside: Every floor has three big flats and upswept balconies. The jagged top holds penthouses of up to three storeys, with roof gardens.
Cromwell Tower.getting_in: Street-level entrance on Cromwell Place, with a staffed foyer

Lauderdale Tower.lede: It stands where the Scottish earls of Lauderdale once kept their London house.
Lauderdale Tower.named_after: The Earls of Lauderdale, Scottish nobles
Lauderdale Tower.namesake: The first earl, John Maitland, was made earl in 1624. His family's London house stood on this spot.
Lauderdale Tower.setting: The westernmost tower, close to Aldersgate Street and Barbican station. Its flats look over Thomas More Garden.
Lauderdale Tower.inside: Three big flats on each floor, each with living rooms in the corners. Three penthouse maisonettes sit at the jagged top, with roof gardens. The tower turns up in the TV drama Luther.
Lauderdale Tower.getting_in: Street-level entrance on Lauderdale Place, off Beech Street, with a staffed foyer

Shakespeare Tower.lede: For years it was the highest block of flats in Europe.
Shakespeare Tower.namesake: Shakespeare lodged with the Mountjoy family, who lived near the Barbican.
Shakespeare Tower.setting: The centre tower, just west of the Barbican Centre. It stands on the south podium and links to the north one.
Shakespeare Tower.inside: Three large flats on each floor, all with upswept balconies. Three penthouse maisonettes at the top have roof gardens.
Shakespeare Tower.getting_in: Main entrance off Defoe Place, with a second off Beech Garden

Andrewes House.lede: Its garden flats are the only ones on the estate with their own gardens.
Andrewes House.namesake: He became vicar of St Giles Cripplegate in 1589. People said he spoke fifteen languages.
Andrewes House.setting: It runs along the south side of the lake. Living rooms face south over Fore Street and bedrooms face north over the water.
Andrewes House.inside: Top-floor penthouses have barrel-vaulted roofs. Two floors of garden flats sit below the podium, each with a patio behind a high wall.
Andrewes House.getting_in: Entrances on Andrewes Highwalk, with stairs and lifts down to Fore Street and Wood Street

Ben Jonson House.lede: It is the longest block on the estate, and it steps right over Golden Lane.
Ben Jonson House.namesake: He was taken out of school to lay bricks like his stepfather. He joined the army in Flanders, killed a Spanish soldier in single combat, then took up the theatre.
Ben Jonson House.setting: The block lies across the north of the estate. The north side looks at the Golden Lane Estate and a school playground. The south side faces the Barbican Centre.
Ben Jonson House.inside: Most flats are maisonettes with stairs inside. Penthouses run to two or three storeys, with arched glass rooms on the roof. A dolphin fountain stands at the front.
Ben Jonson House.getting_in: Three lifts, at the west end, centre and east end, down to Bridgewater Street, Beech Street and Whitecross Street

Breton House.lede: Nearly all its flats are studios, topped by a row of penthouse maisonettes.
Breton House.namesake: He was the son of a rich merchant of Red Cross Street, which now lies buried under the estate. His stepfather was the poet George Gascoigne.
Breton House.setting: It forms the north edge of the estate, at right angles to Ben Jonson House. The east flats look over Whitecross Street. The west flats look over Cripplegate Library and Golden Lane.
Breton House.inside: There are 99 studios and 12 penthouse maisonettes with arched glass roofs. Each entrance is up an outdoor stair to a lobby serving five flats.
Breton House.getting_in: Raised entrances up outdoor stairs, with lifts inside

Defoe House.lede: Daniel Foe was born in this parish and added the "De" to his name himself.
Defoe House.named_after: Daniel Defoe, novelist, spy and journalist (1660–1731)
Defoe House.namesake: He was born Daniel Foe in the parish of St Giles Cripplegate. He added the "De" later. Say the block's name De-FOE.
Defoe House.setting: It lies along the north side of Thomas More Garden. Living rooms face south over the garden and lake. Bedrooms face north towards Shakespeare Tower.
Defoe House.inside: Twenty-four penthouses on the roof have barrel-vaulted ceilings. Garden flats below the podium look over Thomas More Garden.
Defoe House.getting_in: Glazed doors on Defoe Place, one for each of the twelve staircases

Gilbert House.lede: It stands on tall stilts in the lake, with a bridge running underneath.
Gilbert House.namesake: He lived in Redcross Street, whose old route runs right beneath this block. He was Walter Raleigh's half-brother and a champion of the north-west passage.
Gilbert House.setting: The block straddles the lake. West flats look over the Barbican Centre terrace and the water. East flats look over the waterfall towards Willoughby House.
Gilbert House.inside: Flats run from one to five rooms, with penthouses on top. A pub called Crowders sits under the south end of the bridge.
Gilbert House.getting_in: Main entrance on Gilbert Bridge, at podium level

Mountjoy House.lede: Its columns are unusually tall, and the whole block floats above Mountjoy Close.
Mountjoy House.namesake: Shakespeare lodged with the Mountjoy family. Christopher Mountjoy was a French wigmaker.
Mountjoy House.setting: It runs north to south, joined to Thomas More House at an angle. East flats look over the small lake, the City Wall and the old bastion. West flats look over a girls' school.
Mountjoy House.inside: Flats run from two to five rooms, much like those in Gilbert House. Penthouse maisonettes sit on the roof.
Mountjoy House.getting_in: Stairs and lifts at the north and south ends

Seddon House.lede: George Seddon turned a house on Aldersgate Street into England's first big furniture store.
Seddon House.namesake: He converted London House, on Aldersgate Street, into the first big furniture store in England.
Seddon House.setting: It runs from Lauderdale Tower to Thomas More House. Rooms face west over Thomas More Garden or east over Aldersgate Street.
Seddon House.inside: Flats range from studios to five-room penthouse maisonettes. The tall columns and granite-faced lift lobbies stand out at the north end.
Seddon House.getting_in: Entrances at both ends, with the main one on Seddon Highwalk

Speed House.lede: It was the first Barbican block to be built.
Speed House.namesake: He was probably born in St Paul's churchyard and trained as a tailor. The patronage of Sir Fulk Greville freed him to draw maps.
Speed House.setting: It sits in the north-east corner and forms the north edge of Speed Gardens. Living rooms look south over the garden and the lake.
Speed House.inside: Below the podium are two-storey garden maisonettes with their own car ports. Penthouses on top have barrel vaults.
Speed House.getting_in: Doors on Speed Highwalk, with street access from Silk Street beside the Guildhall School

Thomas More House.lede: Its garden flats face the largest garden on the estate.
Thomas More House.named_after: Sir Thomas More, lawyer, statesman and saint (1478–1535)
Thomas More House.namesake: He was born in Milk Street. He called himself the King's good servant, but God's first.
Thomas More House.setting: The block lies along Thomas More Garden. Living rooms above the podium face south over the tennis courts of a girls' school. The north side looks over the garden.
Thomas More House.inside: Three storeys of garden flats sit below the podium, the lowest ones studios. Penthouses crown the top.
Thomas More House.getting_in: Glazed doors on Thomas More Highwalk, and gates onto the garden

Willoughby House.lede: Its flats are rarely identical, and most are maisonettes that go up and over.
Willoughby House.namesake: In 1533 she married Charles Brandon, who owned the manor of Barbican. The block revives the name of the old Willoughby House that stood here.
Willoughby House.setting: It marks the eastern edge of the estate, running from Speed House to Andrewes House. Living rooms face west over the lake. Bedrooms face east towards Moor Lane.
Willoughby House.inside: Most flats are maisonettes with stairs that go up and over. Penthouse maisonettes sit above them.
Willoughby House.getting_in: Main entrances on Willoughby Highwalk, with lifts at both ends and the centre

Bryer Court.lede: It is the narrowest block on the estate.
Bryer Court.named_after: W. Bryer & Sons, gold refiners and assayers
Bryer Court.namesake: The firm worked at 53–54 Barbican. A frieze showing how they refined gold was saved from their building and now hangs in White Lyon Court.
Bryer Court.setting: The block runs north to south on the north podium. All its flats face west and look at Murray House. A small pool with fountains sits at the front.
Bryer Court.inside: Every flat is a studio, and they are nearly identical. An access gallery runs along the back.
Bryer Court.getting_in: Single entrance at the south end, reached by the Fann Street ramp

Bunyan Court.lede: Most of its flats are two-storey maisonettes laid out on a scissor plan.
Bunyan Court.named_after: John Bunyan, writer and Baptist preacher (1628–1688)
Bunyan Court.namesake: He was the son of a Bedford tinker and became a tinker himself. He never went to school but learnt to read and write at home.
Bunyan Court.setting: It runs east to west on the north podium, the middle of a U with John Trundle Court and Bryer Court. North flats overlook Blake Tower. South flats overlook Beech Gardens.
Bunyan Court.inside: Maisonettes have paired balconies on levels 2, 3 and 5. A fitness centre sits under the podium, beside a round fountain pool.
Bunyan Court.getting_in: Entrance and lift at the Bryer Court end, built over the Fann Street ramp

John Trundle Court.lede: Trundle published a pirate edition of Hamlet in 1603.
John Trundle Court.namesake: He published the "bad quarto" of Hamlet in 1603, a rough pirate copy, with Nicholas Ling.
John Trundle Court.setting: It runs north to south along Aldersgate Street on the western edge. West flats look over the street and Barbican station. East flats look over Beech Gardens.
John Trundle Court.inside: There are 117 studios and 16 duplex penthouses with glazed rooms on the roof. A gym sits partly under the block.
John Trundle Court.getting_in: Mezzanine entrances up tiled steps, and a lift down to Aldersgate Street near the bridge to the station

Frobisher Crescent.lede: It was built as flats, spent years as offices, and became flats again in 2010.
Frobisher Crescent.named_after: Sir Martin Frobisher, Elizabethan seaman and privateer
Frobisher Crescent.namesake: Frobisher was picked to test Humphrey Gilbert's idea of a north-west passage. He also held a privateering licence from Elizabeth I.
Frobisher Crescent.setting: The crescent lies between Shakespeare Tower and the Barbican Centre. Flats look onto a sculpture court inside the curve.
Frobisher Crescent.inside: The studios and one- to three-bed flats all have balconies, and end flats wrap round in terraces. Top-floor flats have barrel-arched roofs with mezzanines.
Frobisher Crescent.getting_in: Linked to the Barbican Centre on the east side

Brandon Mews.lede: These small houses sit below the podium, right beside the waterfall that drops into the lake.
Brandon Mews.named_after: The Brandon family, lords of the manor of Barbican
Brandon Mews.namesake: Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk, held the manor. Earlier, Robert Brandon, son of Lord Ufford, had acquired it.
Brandon Mews.setting: The houses face west over the lake, behind the waterfall, or over Speed Garden.
Brandon Mews.inside: Each is a two-storey house with an inside bathroom and angled roof lights. Brown perspex canopies went on in the 1980s.
Brandon Mews.getting_in: Down from the podium on Willoughby Highwalk, with one entrance for every two houses

Lambert Jones Mews.lede: These are the only homes on the estate with back doors that open straight onto a garden.
Lambert Jones Mews.namesake: In 1824 he put a motion to the Court of Common Council that led to the founding of the Guildhall Library.
Lambert Jones Mews.setting: The houses face east onto Thomas More Garden. Their front doors open onto a cobbled mews road.
Lambert Jones Mews.inside: Each is a two-storey house with a garage and a roof garden.
Lambert Jones Mews.getting_in: Front doors on a cobbled mews road below Lauderdale Place

The Postern.lede: Its front doors open onto a covered bridge, and the houses look over St Giles church.
The Postern.named_after: The posterns, small side gates in the City Wall at Cripplegate
The Postern.namesake: A postern is a back door or side gate. The City Wall had several near here.
The Postern.setting: The houses look over St Giles church and the stretch of lake between the church and the City Wall.
The Postern.inside: Most are long, narrow town houses with garages, open-tread stairs and roof gardens. The row also holds the rectory of St Giles.
The Postern.getting_in: Front doors on the covered Postern Bridge, with stairs down to St Giles Terrace

Wallside.lede: It is the only part of the estate where the homes face outward to the street.
Wallside.named_after: The Roman and City Wall beside it
Wallside.namesake: The block runs parallel to surviving stretches of the old wall.
Wallside.setting: The fronts look over Bridgewater Square. The backs look over St Giles Terrace, the lake and the City Wall.
Wallside.inside: These are town houses with garages and roof terraces. One holds a doctor's surgery and another a dentist's.
Wallside.getting_in: Street doors on the square, with upper entrances from the highwalk
